narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 51% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability tipped just over 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

Three factors drove this outcome, ranked by importance. First, your undergraduate GPA of 3.30 actually worked in your favor. It is slightly above the average of students who were accepted, and the model saw this as a meaningful signal that you could succeed. Unfortunately, that positive push was not strong enough to overcome the other influences.

The second most important factor was your class ranking in the third year of law school. Placing in the second decile (compared to an average around the sixth decile for accepted students) signaled to the model that you may struggle to keep pace with your classmates. This ranking pulled the prediction strongly toward failure.

Third, your family income bracket of lower-middle also nudged the outcome toward rejection. While many accepted students come from upper-middle or middle-income families, only about 9% share your lower-middle background, and the model interpreted this as an additional risk factor for bar exam performance.

Taken together, your solid college grades were outweighed by weaker law-school performance and socioeconomic signals. To improve your chances, focus on raising your class rank in the remaining years, seek academic support early, and consider retaking the LSAT if possible. Strengthening these areas will directly address the factors that led to this decision. (248 words)
